title: Service Decomposition
summary: How to draw service boundaries by business capability instead of technical layer, and the warning signs a boundary is in the wrong place.

slides.markdown:
Where you draw service boundaries decides everything else about how well microservices work — get it wrong and you get a [monolith-vs-microservices](monolith-vs-microservices) split that carries all the network cost with none of the independence benefit.

The core rule: decompose by **business capability**, not by technical layer. A boundary is right when a team can change and deploy their service without a meeting with three other teams first.

slides.sectionTitle: Decomposing by business capability, not by technical layer
slides.markdown:
A **technical-layer split** carves services along the tech stack: a "UI service," a "business-logic service," a "database service." It feels natural to engineers, but it means almost every user action — say, placing an order — has to hop across all three services, so nothing actually becomes independent.

A **business-capability split** (also called a **bounded context**, from Domain-Driven Design) instead carves along what the business does: Ordering, Inventory, Payments, Shipping. Each service owns the full stack — its own logic and its own data — for one coherent piece of the business.

The test: can you describe the service's job in one sentence a product manager would recognize? "The Orders service tracks and fulfills orders" passes; "the business-logic service" does not.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: wrong (layer-based) vs right (domain-based) service boundaries
slides.markdown:
![Layer-based decomposition crossing all layers vs domain-based staying in one service](assets/layer-vs-domain-decomposition.svg)

The layer-based split forces one user action to cross every service; the domain-based split lets most actions stay within one service's boundary, only reaching out for genuinely cross-domain work.

That's the concrete difference a bounded-context split buys you: fewer network hops per request, and each hop maps to a real cross-team dependency instead of an artifact of how the stack is layered.

assets.alt: Layer-based decomposition crossing all layers vs domain-based staying in one service

slides.sectionTitle: Signs a service boundary is wrong: chatty calls, shared tables
slides.markdown:
Two concrete symptoms tell you a boundary is drawn in the wrong place, faster than any diagram debate.

**Chatty calls**: if handling one user request means Service A calls B, which calls C, which calls back to A, the "services" are really one capability that got sliced arbitrarily. **Shared tables**: if two services read or write the same underlying table, they aren't actually independent — a schema change in one silently breaks the other, and you've built a distributed monolith with extra latency.

Either symptom means the same fix: merge the pieces back into one service, or find the real seam and move the shared logic or data fully to one side of it.

slides.sectionTitle: Sizing a service: the two-pizza team and single-responsibility at service level
slides.markdown:
There's no fixed line count for "right-sized," but two heuristics help. **Two-pizza team** (Amazon's rule): a service should be ownable by a team small enough to feed with two pizzas — roughly 6-10 people — so ownership stays clear and coordination stays cheap. **Single-responsibility at the service level**: a service should have one reason to change — if you find yourself explaining a service's purpose with "and" three times ("it handles orders, and inventory, and also some reporting"), it's really three services wearing one name.

Err toward fewer, coarser services early — splitting later is far cheaper than merging services that were split too fine and now can't stop calling each other.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: coarse-grained vs fine-grained service boundaries
slides.markdown:
| | Coarse-grained (fewer, bigger services) | Fine-grained (many, small services) |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-service calls per request | Few — most logic stays in-process | Many — a request can fan out across a dozen services |
| Team ownership clarity | Can blur if one team owns several capabilities | Sharp, if each service maps to one real capability |
| Operational overhead | Lower — fewer deployables to run and monitor | Higher — more deploy pipelines, more on-call surfaces |
| Risk of "distributed monolith" | Low | High, if boundaries were drawn too eagerly |

**How to decide:** start coarser than feels aggressive — a service per real bounded context, not per database table or per class — and split further only when a specific piece needs independent scaling, deployment, or ownership.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a distributed monolith — services that must deploy together
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have ten separate services in ten separate repos, so we've done microservices right."

**Why it's wrong:** if changing Service A routinely requires changing and redeploying Service B in lockstep — because they share a database table, or one's API contract is too brittle to version independently — you have a **distributed monolith**: all the network latency and operational overhead of microservices, with none of the independent-deployability benefit that justified the split.

**Correct model:** the test for "real" service independence isn't how many repos exist, it's whether you can deploy any one service on its own, on its own schedule, without coordinating a joint release with another team.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: sizing a service around a team that can operate it
slides.subTitle: Estimation
slides.markdown:
A useful sizing heuristic is a two-pizza team (roughly 6-10 engineers) owning a service they can fully understand, deploy, and be on-call for without constant cross-team check-ins. If a "service" needs more than that to operate — say, 20+ engineers touching one deployable — it's usually still a monolith wearing a service's name. If a service is small enough that one engineer owns it alone with almost no traffic to justify its own pipeline, on-call rotation, and monitoring, the operational overhead per unit of business value is often too high, and it's a candidate for merging back into a neighbor.

Concrete example: a "notifications" service handling under 100 requests/sec, owned by one engineer, with its own deploy pipeline, dashboard, and alerting, might cost more in maintenance overhead (patching, dependency upgrades, on-call burden) than the isolation is worth — folding it into the service that triggers most of its notifications often nets out better until it genuinely needs independent scaling.

The takeaway: service count isn't free — each one carries a fixed operational tax, so size services around a team that can actually absorb that tax, not around the smallest coherent chunk of domain logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: decomposing before the domain is understood
slides.markdown:
Decomposing services before the domain is well understood is a common and expensive mistake — the "signs a boundary is wrong" slide above (chatty calls, shared tables) are usually the visible symptom of decomposing *too early*, while the team's mental model of the domain was still shifting.

Concrete example: a team splits "orders" and "billing" into separate services in month one of a new product, guessing at the boundary — three months later, once real usage reveals that pricing rules need order-line detail on every billing calculation, the two services end up making a synchronous call to each other on nearly every request, effectively re-coupling them but now with network calls and two deploy pipelines instead of one. The fix at that point (re-merging or redrawing the boundary) costs far more than waiting three more months to decompose with the pricing-rules coupling already known would have.

**Testing:** whether you can recognize premature decomposition as a real failure mode — sometimes the correct answer to "how should we split this" is "not yet, we don't know the domain well enough."
